title: API latency increased from 100ms to 4 seconds: how do you investigate?
description: Learn a systematic approach to diagnosing sudden latency spikes in production APIs, from metrics to database to infrastructure.

data.text: Sudden latency spikes are among the most stressful production incidents. A healthy API that normally responds in 100 milliseconds jumping to 4 seconds means something changed — and you need to find it fast. The key is to follow a layered investigation rather than guessing.

Start by confirming the symptom. Is the latency increase global or limited to a specific endpoint, region, or user segment? Use your monitoring dashboard to compare p50, p95, and p99 latencies. A spike in p99 with a stable p50 usually indicates a subset of slow requests, not a universal degradation.

items: Layer 1: Check for recent deployments, config changes, or feature flags that flipped on.
Layer 2: Look at infrastructure — CPU, memory, disk I/O, network, and connection pool saturation.
Layer 3: Examine downstream dependencies: database query times, external API calls, and message queues.
Layer 4: Profile the application code path for the affected endpoint to find the exact bottleneck.

data.text: The database is the most common culprit for sudden latency increases. Begin by comparing the slow query log before and after the regression. Look for queries that changed execution plans, new missing-index warnings, or blocking chains.

data.title: SQL Server: Identify the top slow queries since the regression
data.code:
SELECT TOP 20
    qs.sql_handle,
    qs.execution_count,
    qs.total_elapsed_time / 1000000.0 AS total_seconds,
    qs.avg_elapsed_time / 1000000.0 AS avg_seconds,
    SUBSTRING(st.text, (qs.statement_start_offset / 2) + 1,
        (CASE WHEN qs.statement_end_offset = -1
              THEN LEN(CONVERT(NVARCHAR(MAX), st.text)) * 2
              ELSE qs.statement_end_offset END - qs.statement_start_offset) / 2 + 1) AS query_text
FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats AS qs
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) AS st
WHERE qs.last_execution_time >= DATEADD(MINUTE, -30, GETUTCDATE())
ORDER BY qs.total_elapsed_time DESC;

data.title: Do not restart the service to confirm
data.text: Restarting clears symptoms but also destroys evidence — connection pool state, in-flight queries, and deadlock graphs. Investigate first, restart only after you understand the root cause.

If the database looks healthy, instrument the application. Add structured logging with elapsed milliseconds per step. In ASP.NET Core, use DiagnosticSource or a middleware timer to separate network time from database time from business-logic time.

data.title: C#: Minimal request-timing middleware

items: New code path that skips caching or executes redundant queries.
Deployment that changed connection-string settings or timeout values.
Schema migration that invalidated cached query plans.
Traffic pattern change combined with undersized connection pools.
Index corruption or auto-statistics update triggered by large data changes.

items.text: Confirm the symptom with quantitative data before investigating.
items.hint: Mention p50, p95, p99 and endpoint-level breakdown.

items.text: Rule out recent deployments and feature flags first.
items.hint: Speed of elimination matters in an interview.

items.text: Separate application, database, and infrastructure concerns.
Propose concrete SQL and code-level diagnostics.
Mention observability: metrics, logs, and distributed traces.
items.hint: Modern backends rely on all three.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Start with data, not guesses: confirm the latency spike with monitoring before opening any tool.
Layer your investigation: deployment, infrastructure, dependencies, then application code.
The database is the most common source of sudden regressions — check query plans and indexes first.
Instrumentation is your best long-term defense against latency mysteries.
data.takeaway: Investigate systematically from metrics to code, preserving evidence before changing anything.
